title: Bittersweet Glass
warm:
The promise was made at the corridor window, at the far end of the hall, where the glass ran floor to ceiling and the city lay below like something spilled.

"When it's over," Nolan Greer said.

"When it's over," [player_name] agreed.

Neither of them said what *it* was. They didn't need to. It was Detective Imani Brooks's file, still open, still thickening. It was the holding board's inquiry into Nolan's conduct, which his lawyers said would take a year and which Marcus Pell privately said might take three. It was the reporters who still waited some mornings at the curb where the black car used to idle. It was Vivienne.

Mostly it was Vivienne.

Because nothing had settled. Not after everything—not after the broadcast, or the glass dawn, or the long nights of choosing. If anything, the harder [player_name] looked, the more doors opened. A woman matching Vivienne's description had been seen in Milan, at a boutique that sold the same perfume; the witness later wasn't sure. A Zurich account in her name had been drawn on twice, then gone dormant; Brooks couldn't say who had drawn it. The plane-desk handler's logs showed one passenger too few on a flight to the coast and a lawyer too many at every interview. And an inland landlord swore a woman had rented an apartment from him months before the fourteenth, paid in cash, left it spotless, and vanished—as if she had been rehearsing.

Willing. Paid. Dead. Staged.

[player_name] turned the four words over at night like stones in a pocket. Some nights one was heavier. Some nights another. She had stopped expecting any of them to become the only one.

So they had made the promise. Not to marry. Not to stop. Only to wait. Nolan would stay in his penthouse, and she would stay in hers, and neither of them would cross the other's threshold until Brooks closed the file or the board closed its inquiry or Vivienne walked through the lobby doors and signed Rhea Quinn's slate—until something, anything, finished.

Until then, they had the hall.

Every night at eleven, she came out of her door with two glasses and he came out of his with the bottle, and they met at the corridor window. They stood side by side with their shoulders almost touching and drank one glass each and talked. About the day. About the inquiry. About a book she was reading and a deal he was losing. Sometimes about Vivienne, carefully, the way you might touch a bruise to see if it still hurt. Sometimes about nothing at all.

Then, at midnight, they walked the twelve steps back—six each—and went into their separate doors.

It was the strangest love she had ever known. It was also, in some ways, the most honest. There was no soft alibi in it. No cover. Just two people who wanted each other badly and had decided that wanting was not yet enough, standing in a hallway with the whole city throwing its light up at them like an accusation they had agreed to hear out.

Rhea, who saw everything, asked her once in the lobby: "Is it hard?"

"Every night," [player_name] said.

"Then why?"

She thought about it. "Because when we finally cross," she said, "I want there to be nothing on the other side of the door but him."

In the spring, Brooks called to say the Milan lead was dead. In the summer, the board extended its inquiry. In the fall, the Zurich account moved again—one withdrawal, a small amount, from a machine in a country Vivienne had never been known to visit. Brooks didn't know what it meant. Nobody did.

The promise held. It frayed at the edges some nights—his hand finding hers on the window ledge and staying there too long; her head tipping, once, onto his shoulder, and both of them standing very still until she lifted it again—but it held.

Tonight it was October again. The fourteenth. A year.

She came out at eleven with two glasses. He was already at the window, the bottle unopened in his hand, his reflection faint over the city lights.

"I've been thinking," he said, not turning around, "that it may never be over."

She stopped beside him. The glass was cold. The city below was a million lit windows and not one of them knew where Vivienne Greer was.

"I know," she said.

"Brooks may never close it. The board may never finish. She may never come back, or be found, or—" He stopped. "I could be sixty. You could be forty-five. We could be standing at this window with two glasses and a bottle, still waiting for someone else's ending to give us permission for ours."

"So what are you saying?"

He turned then and looked at her. The city light caught one side of his face and left the other in shadow, and for once he didn't look brutal or charming or polished. He looked like a man about to ask for something he could not buy.

"I'm saying I don't want to wait for her ending anymore." His voice was low. "I want to know if you'll let me write ours without one."

Down the shaft, soft and silver, the private elevator chimed.

Neither of them moved. The glasses were in her hands, empty. The bottle was in his, unopened. Behind them, twelve steps of carpet ran back toward two doors—his, and hers—both closed, both waiting.

[player_name] looked at him for a long moment. Then she set the glasses down on the window ledge, very carefully, side by side.

"Ask me properly," she said.
hot:
The promise was simple: no doors.

Not his, not hers. Neither of them would cross the other's threshold until it was over—until Detective Imani Brooks closed the file, or the holding board closed its inquiry into Nolan Greer, or Vivienne walked into the lobby and signed Rhea Quinn's slate. Until something finished.

Nothing finished. Vivienne stayed four stories at once. A possible sighting in Milan that fell apart. A Zurich account that moved, went still, moved again. A handler's log with one passenger too few. An inland apartment rented in cash months before the fourteenth, left spotless, as if someone had rehearsed. Willing. Paid. Dead. Staged. [player_name] carried all four under her ribs and had stopped expecting any of them to be the only one.

So they had the hall.

Every night at eleven they met at the corridor window at the far end, floor-to-ceiling glass, the city spilled out below. One glass each. Talk. At midnight, six steps each back to their own doors.

That was the promise. The promise did not say anything about what happened at the window.

It started with his hand on hers on the ledge, staying too long. Then her head on his shoulder. Then one night in February she turned and kissed him, and he made a sound like something breaking, and pressed her back against the cold glass and kissed her until her knees went weak. They stood there for an hour, mouths and hands, fully clothed, his thigh between hers, her grinding against it shamelessly with the whole city at her back. She came like that, rocking on his leg, her face in his neck, and he held her through it shaking with how badly he wanted more.

"No doors," he said hoarsely into her hair.

"No doors," she agreed. And then, because she was cruel and wanted him to suffer as much as she did: "The promise didn't say anything about the hall."

He went very still. Then he laughed, low and helpless, and dropped his forehead against hers.

After that the hall became theirs in a way it had never been.

Some nights it was just the window and the wine. Some nights it was his hand under her skirt against the glass, two fingers deep inside her, his thumb working her clit while she bit his shoulder to stay quiet and the elevator hummed somewhere in the shaft. Some nights she knelt on the carpet with her back to the city and took him in her mouth, slow, looking up at him while his palms pressed flat against the window on either side of her head and he said her name like a prayer he didn't believe in.

And once—only once, the night the board extended its inquiry again—he lifted her onto the wide window ledge, pushed her dress up, and fucked her right there against the glass. Hard and desperate and far too loud, her legs locked around his hips, the cold window at her back and the heat of him inside her, the city blazing behind her like it was watching. She came clenching around him with her nails in his neck. He came with his face buried in her throat, groaning her name, hips jerking, holding her like he was afraid she'd fall thirty floors.

Then they fixed their clothes. And walked the twelve steps. Six each. And went into separate doors.

That was the bittersweet of it. Everything, and not home.

Some nights, alone in her own bed after midnight, she could still feel him inside her and hear his door click shut across the hall, and she'd lie there aching and furious and in love, listening to the building settle, wondering if he was awake twelve steps away with his hand where hers was. She never asked. Asking would have been a door.

Tonight was the fourteenth of October. A year. She came out at eleven with two glasses and found him already at the window, bottle unopened, his reflection faint over the lights.

"It may never be over," he said without turning.

"I know."

"I could be sixty. You could be forty-five. Still out here with two glasses, waiting for her ending to give us permission for ours." He turned. City light cut across his face. He didn't look brutal or polished. He looked like a man about to ask for something he couldn't buy. "I don't want to wait for her ending anymore. I want to write ours without one."

Down the shaft, soft and silver, the elevator chimed.

Her whole body answered him—pulse, breath, the familiar ache low and insistent. Behind them, twelve steps of carpet ran back to two closed doors.

She set the glasses down on the ledge, side by side.

"Ask me properly," she said, "and then take me through your door."
